Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Willmore Mountain Goat Surveys (2024)
Background 
Aerial surveys for mountain goats have been 
conducted in the Willmore Wilderness Park and 
adjacent areas since 1974. The goal of these surveys 
is to collect data on population trends, distribution, and 
herd composition, and to monitor the status of these 
mountain goat populations given their sensitivity to 
harvest.  
The objective of the mountain goat surveys in 2024 
was to inform the status of mountain goat populations 
in Goat Hunting Areas (Fig. 1) within the Northwest 
Region where a mountain goat season has been 
reinstated, and complexes where the survey 
information was required to assess the effects of 
management actions (i.e. supplemental mineral lick 
provisioning on Llama-Turret).  
Survey Method 
Surveys of Ptarmigan lake, Mt. Deveber, Llama-Turret, 
North Persimmon, and Monoghan mountain 
complexes (Fig. 2) were completed using an AS350 
helicopter with three observers and the pilot. A sliding 
door that could be opened on the left side was used to 
increase the detection of animals below the aircraft. 
Transects were completed in a counter-clockwise 
direction around each mountain complex between 
timberline and ridge top to maximize the visibility for 
the two left observers. Transects were established by 
following the alpine contour, and multiple transects 
were often required to ensure complete coverage in 
areas of large or complex terrain, or where visibility 
was otherwise obscured (e.g. higher tree cover, finer 
scale terrain features). Front left and rear left 
passengers were responsible for navigating, 
classifying, and taking photos to confirm classification. 
Flight began early in the morning when temperatures 
were coolest, and winds were minimal to maximize 
conditions for detecting animals. After the survey, 
group photographs were used to confirm or improve 
the field classification, where possible.  
To assess trends in local population abundance, we 
compared annual total counts of non-kids (adult and 
yearling mountain goats), herein referred to as adults, 
to the long-term average for each of the complexes. At 
the regional scale, we used a relative population index 
to assess trends in abundance through time. This 
index was calculated by dividing the total number of 
adults observed in all complexes flown in a given year 
by the sum of the long-term averages for those 
complexes. For reference, an index value of 1 
represents the average observed mountain goat 
abundance for all years, 0.5 and 2.0 represent half and 
double the average mountain goat abundance for the 
region, respectively. We assessed regional trends in 
annual kid productivity by pooling ratio estimates 
across complexes that were surveyed in each year. 
Surveys to inventory the total count for bighorn sheep 
are conducted in winter, when their distribution is 
concentrated and snow conditions facilitate higher 
detection, however we report the count and 
composition of incidental observations from the 
survey. 
Results 
Surveys were completed from July 6 – July 10, 2024, 
with a survey effort of 35.2 hours of flight time. A total 
of 493 mountain goats were observed from 108 
independent groups across all surveyed complexes. 
Of this total, 333 adults, 47 yearlings, and 109 kids 
were observed (Table 1). Four mountain goats were 
left unclassified. Not all ranges are above the long-
term average, however, all of the populations have 
increased since the most recent 2021 survey (Figures 
3 and 4). Incidental observations of bighorn sheep 
during the mountain goat survey included a total of 
439 bighorn sheep were observed of which 188 were 
ewes (and some yearling rams), 93 were lambs, 92 
were rams and 39 were unclassified adults.
